chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Binary World
pages: Computers are built on millions of tiny electronic switches called transistors. These switches have only two states: ON or OFF.
In mathematics, we represent these states as numbers: 1 for ON and 0 for OFF. This base-2 number system is called binary.
Every letter, number, and picture you see is encoded in binary. For example, the letter 'A' is stored as the binary byte 01000001.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The CPU & Memory
pages: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the brain of the computer. It executes instructions using the Fetch-Execute cycle.
First, the CPU fetches an instruction from RAM (Random Access Memory), decodes what it means, and then executes it.
RAM is temporary storage. It holds active programs. When the computer turns off, all data in RAM is cleared.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Global Network
pages: The Internet connects computers worldwide. Information is broken down into small units called packets.
Each packet has a header containing the sender and receiver's IP addresses. Routers direct these packets across the network.
Once all packets arrive at the destination, they are reassembled into the original file or web page.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Variables and Math
pages: Coding is writing instructions for a computer. We store data in named slots called variables.
Think of a variable as a labeled box. You can put a value inside: score = 10, name = 'Mentor'.
You can change the value later. Math operators (+, -, *, /) modify number variables: score = score + 5.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Control Flow & Logic
pages: Computers make decisions using 'if' statements. These statements check a conditional expression.
For example: 'if (gold >= 50) { buyHat(); } else { showWarning(); }'. Only one path is run.
Boolean logic uses AND (&&), OR (||), and NOT (!) operators to combine multiple conditions.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Repeating with Loops
pages: Instead of writing the same instruction ten times, coders use loops to repeat code blocks.
A 'while' loop runs as long as a condition is true. Be careful to update the condition to avoid infinite loops!
A 'for' loop runs a specific number of times, typically incrementing a counter variable from 0 to a target limit.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Speed Multiplication
pages: Mental math is the practice of performing math calculations in your head without using a calculator or paper.
To multiply a two-digit number by 11: add the two digits and place the sum in the middle. E.g., 23 * 11 -> 2 + 3 = 5, result is 253.
If the sum is 10 or more, carry 1 over to the left digit. E.g., 85 * 11 -> 8 + 5 = 13, result is 935.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Division Shortcuts
pages: A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. E.g., 168 -> 1 + 6 + 8 = 15 (divisible by 3).
A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. E.g., 1024 -> 24 (divisible by 4).
A number is divisible by 6 if it is even and divisible by 3. E.g., 312 is even and 3+1+2=6, so it is divisible by 6.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Visual Estimation
pages: Estimation helps you quickly check if an answer is reasonable. Round numbers to the nearest ten or hundred first.
To estimate 392 + 507, calculate 400 + 500 = 900. The exact answer is 899, which is extremely close.
This mental baseline allows engineers and scientists to detect scale errors instantly.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Tectonic Dynamics
pages: The Earth's crust is not solid. It is divided into large moving slabs called tectonic plates.
These plates float on the hot mantle below. When plates collide, they form mountains or volcanic arcs.
When plates slide past each other, friction causes stress to build. The sudden release of this stress causes earthquakes.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Atmosphere
pages: Our atmosphere consists of nitrogen (78%), oxygen (21%), and trace gases. It protects us from cosmic radiation.
Air rises at the equator and falls at the poles, forming huge circulation cells that drive global wind patterns.
The greenhouse effect traps solar heat in the lower atmosphere, keeping the Earth warm enough to sustain life.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Water Cycles
pages: Water moves constantly between oceans, atmosphere, and land. This continuous loop is the hydrological cycle.
Solar energy causes evaporation. Water vapor rises, cools, and condenses into clouds.
Precipitation (rain/snow) returns water to the surface, filling rivers and recharging underground aquifers.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Sentence Structures
pages: A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb, and must express a complete thought. E.g., 'The player ran.'
A clause is a group of words with a subject and verb. Independent clauses can stand alone as sentences.
Dependent clauses cannot stand alone. They must be joined to an independent clause: 'Because the forest was dark, the player ran.'

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Active vs. Passive Voice
pages: In the active voice, the subject performs the action. E.g., 'The hero chopped the tree.' This style is direct and clear.
In the passive voice, the target receives the action. E.g., 'The tree was chopped by the hero.' This style is slower.
Use the active voice to make your writing feel more dynamic, and save the passive voice for when the actor is unknown.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Punctuation Rules
pages: Punctuation adds rhythm and structure. A comma separates items in a list and joins clauses with a conjunction.
A semicolon connects two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction: 'The forest was dark; the caves were quiet.'
Never use consecutive commas or run-on sentences. Keep your structures clear for high readability.
